questions.question: How do you write a unit test for a Spring @Service using Mockito?
questions.title: Unit Test Spring Service Mockito | Java Fresher Interview
questions.direct_answer: Use @ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class) to run the test with Mockito, @Mock to create a mock repository, and @InjectMocks to inject that mock into your service. This is a true unit test—no Spring context loads, runs in milliseconds. Only use @SpringBootTest when you need the full application context for integration testing.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand the difference between a fast unit test and a Spring integration test, and can avoid loading the full context unnecessarily
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Adding @SpringBootTest to every service test, which loads the entire Spring context and makes the test suite 50-100x slower
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Show a complete unit test with proper assertions and explain that avoiding Spring context startup is the key to a fast test suite

sections.title: Unit Testing Spring Services Without Spring Context
sections.content: **A true unit test for a Spring service does not load the Spring context at all.** The service is just a Java class with business logic; its dependencies (like repositories) are mocked using Mockito. You use **@ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class)** to enable Mockito annotations, **@Mock** to create mock dependencies, and **@InjectMocks** to automatically inject those mocks into your service instance. This approach is extremely fast—tests run in milliseconds because there's no framework startup overhead. **Think of it like testing a calculator:** you don't need to boot an entire operating system to verify that 2+2=4. Similarly, you don't need Spring's dependency injection container just to test that OrderService.calculateTotal() adds up prices correctly. Reserve @SpringBootTest for true integration tests where you need actual database connections, HTTP endpoints, or multiple layers working together.

sections.title: Complete Unit Test for OrderService
Key Points
content: **@ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class)**: Enables Mockito annotations in JUnit 5 tests without loading Spring context
**@Mock**: Creates a Mockito mock of the dependency (repository, client, etc.) that records and verifies interactions
**@InjectMocks**: Tells Mockito to instantiate the service and inject all @Mock dependencies into it automatically
**when().thenReturn()**: Stubs the mock's behavior so calling findById returns your test data instead of null
**verify()**: Asserts that the service actually called the repository method with the expected arguments
**Speed**: Unit tests run in 10-50ms each; @SpringBootTest tests take 3-10 seconds just to start the context
**Scope**: Unit tests verify business logic in isolation; use @SpringBootTest only when testing cross-layer integration

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: I'd use Mockito to write a fast unit test without loading Spring at all. First, I annotate the test class with at-ExtendWith MockitoExtension dot class to enable Mockito's annotations. Then I create a mock of the repository using at-Mock, and I use at-InjectMocks on the service field so Mockito automatically injects that mock repository into the service instance. In the test method, I use when and thenReturn to stub what the repository should return when the service calls it. For example, if I'm testing an OrderService that fetches an order by ID, I'd stub the repository's findById method to return a test Order object. Then I call the service method and assert the result using assertEquals. I also use verify to make sure the service actually called the repository with the correct ID. This approach is really fast because there's no Spring context startup—the test runs in milliseconds. The key mistake freshers make is adding at-SpringBootTest to every service test, which loads the entire application context and makes your test suite incredibly slow. You only need at-SpringBootTest when you're doing a true integration test that requires multiple beans working together or a real database connection. For unit tests, pure Mockito is the right tool.

questions.question: How do you test a Spring REST controller using MockMvc?
questions.title: Spring MockMvc Controller Testing | Java Fresher Interview
questions.direct_answer: Use @WebMvcTest on your test class to load only the Spring MVC layer (controllers, filters, advice). Inject MockMvc to perform HTTP requests in memory. Mock the controller's service dependencies with @MockBean. Use mockMvc.perform() to send requests and andExpect() to assert on status codes, headers, and JSON response body.

interviewer_intent.testing: Practical Spring MVC layer testing—a core skill for Spring Boot REST API development
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using @SpringBootTest and TestRestTemplate when @WebMvcTest with MockMvc is faster and more focused on the controller layer
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Show a complete test with JSON path assertions and explain that @WebMvcTest only loads web layer beans, not services or repositories

sections.title: Testing REST Controllers with MockMvc and @WebMvcTest
sections.content: **@WebMvcTest is a Spring Boot slice test that loads only the web layer**—your controllers, filters, exception handlers, and MVC configuration—without starting a full HTTP server or loading service and repository beans. **MockMvc** is the test client that lets you perform HTTP requests in memory and assert on the response. Think of it like **a flight simulator for your REST API:** you can test all the controls (endpoints, request mappings, response codes) without actually taking off (starting a server). You use **@MockBean** to create mocked versions of the service dependencies your controller needs, then stub their behavior with Mockito's when/thenReturn. MockMvc's fluent API lets you build requests (GET, POST, PUT, DELETE), set headers and JSON bodies, then chain assertions on the response—status code, content type, specific JSON fields using **JsonPath** expressions. This approach is much faster than @SpringBootTest because it doesn't load your entire application, and you don't need an actual HTTP port or network stack.

sections.title: MockMvc Test for OrderController
Key Points
content: **@WebMvcTest**: Spring Boot slice test that loads only controllers, filters, and MVC config—not services or repositories
**MockMvc**: Test client that performs HTTP requests in memory without starting a real server or using network sockets
**@MockBean**: Creates a mock that's registered as a Spring bean, replacing the real service in the controller's dependencies
**perform()**: Starts building an HTTP request—supports get, post, put, delete, patch methods with MockMvcRequestBuilders
**andExpect()**: Chains assertions on the response—status, headers, content type, and JSON body using JsonPath
**JsonPath**: XPath-like syntax for asserting on JSON fields—dollar-sign-dot-fieldName extracts nested values
**Speed advantage**: @WebMvcTest starts in 2-4 seconds versus 8-12 seconds for @SpringBootTest with full context

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: I'd use at-WebMvcTest to test a Spring REST controller because it only loads the web layer, which is much faster than loading the entire application. I annotate the test class with at-WebMvcTest and specify the controller class I'm testing. Spring auto-configures MockMvc for me, so I just inject it with at-Autowired. Since the controller depends on a service, I use at-MockBean to create a mocked version of that service—at-MockBean tells Spring to replace the real service bean with this mock. In the test method, I stub the service's behavior using when and thenReturn from Mockito. For example, if the controller calls orderService dot findById, I stub it to return a test Order object. Then I use mockMvc dot perform with get or post to simulate an HTTP request to the endpoint. I chain andExpect calls to assert the response—status dot isOk checks for 200, content dot contentType verifies the response is JSON, and jsonPath lets me assert on specific JSON fields like dollar-sign dot id or dollar-sign dot item. One common mistake is using at-SpringBootTest for controller tests, which loads your entire application including the database and all services. That's overkill and really slow. At-WebMvcTest is focused—it only loads what you need to test the controller layer, so tests run in a couple seconds instead of ten.

questions.question: How do you test a Spring Data JPA repository?
questions.title: Spring Data JPA Repository Testing | Java Fresher Interview
questions.direct_answer: Use @DataJpaTest to load only the JPA layer with an embedded H2 database. This slice test auto-configures Spring Data JPA repositories, runs each test in a transaction that rolls back after the test completes. Test custom @Query methods, derived query methods, and entity constraints here—no mocking needed.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of JPA repository testing with a real database slice, not mocked repositories
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Trying to test repository query logic by mocking the repository itself, which defeats the purpose—you can't test SQL/JPQL queries against a mock
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain that @DataJpaTest uses an in-memory database and transaction rollback, so tests don't pollute each other and run fast

sections.title: Testing JPA Repositories with @DataJpaTest and Embedded Database
sections.content: **@DataJpaTest is a Spring Boot slice test that loads only the JPA/database layer**—your repositories, entity mappings, and an embedded H2 database—without loading controllers, services, or the full application context. Each test method runs inside a **transaction that automatically rolls back** at the end, so your test data never persists between tests. This is like **a sandbox for database operations:** you can insert, update, query, and delete entities, then the sandbox resets itself. You test real repository behavior here—custom @Query methods, derived query methods (findByEmailAndStatus), entity constraints, and JPA cascade rules. **You cannot test query logic with a mocked repository** because the mock doesn't execute SQL; it only returns what you stub. @DataJpaTest is much faster than @SpringBootTest because it skips the web layer, security, and service beans. The embedded H2 database starts in milliseconds and runs entirely in memory, so tests are fast and don't depend on external database availability.

sections.title: Testing Custom Repository Query with @DataJpaTest
Key Points
content: **@DataJpaTest**: Slice test that loads only JPA repositories, entities, and an embedded H2 database—no web or service layer
**TestEntityManager**: JPA-aware test utility that lets you persist/flush entities directly, bypassing Spring Data methods
**Transaction rollback**: Each test runs in a transaction that rolls back automatically, so data never persists between tests
**Embedded H2**: In-memory database that starts in milliseconds, requires no external setup, and resets after the test class
**Custom queries**: Test @Query methods and derived queries (findByStatusAndCreatedAfter) with real SQL/JPQL execution
**Entity constraints**: Test unique constraints, foreign keys, and cascade operations that only work with a real database
**No mocking**: You test the actual repository implementation and query execution, not a stubbed mock object

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: I'd use at-DataJpaTest to test a Spring Data JPA repository because it loads just the database layer with an embedded H2 database, which is really fast. I annotate the test class with at-DataJpaTest, and Spring auto-configures my repository and a TestEntityManager. Each test method runs inside a transaction that automatically rolls back when the test finishes, so my test data doesn't leak into other tests. To test a custom query, I use TestEntityManager to persist some test entities, call flush to make sure they're written to the database, then call the repository method I'm testing and assert on the results. For example, if I have a findByStatus method, I'd insert a few orders with different statuses, then verify that the query returns only the orders matching the status I passed in. One key point is that you can't test repository queries by mocking the repository itself—a mock just returns whatever you stub it to return. With at-DataJpaTest, you're testing the actual SQL or JPQL query execution against a real database. The embedded H2 database runs entirely in memory and starts in a fraction of a second, so tests are fast. This is much better than using at-SpringBootTest, which would load your entire application and might connect to a real database that needs setup and teardown scripts.

questions.question: What is the difference between @SpringBootTest and slice test annotations?
questions.title: @SpringBootTest vs Slice Tests Spring Boot | Java Fresher
questions.direct_answer: @SpringBootTest loads the entire application context—all beans, all auto-configuration, full Spring Boot environment. Slice tests like @WebMvcTest, @DataJpaTest, @JsonTest load only the relevant layer (web, JPA, JSON serialization). Slice tests are faster and more focused; use @SpringBootTest only for true end-to-end integration tests.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of Spring Boot's layered testing strategy and when to use each approach for speed and focus
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using @SpringBootTest for every test because it's the most familiar annotation, leading to slow test suites
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Name the common slice tests, explain what each loads, and describe a concrete scenario where @SpringBootTest is the right choice

sections.title: Full Context vs. Slice Testing in Spring Boot
sections.content: **@SpringBootTest loads your entire Spring Boot application**—every controller, service, repository, configuration class, auto-configuration, security setup, database connection pool, and any other beans defined in your context. It's like **booting your entire car to test the radio:** technically it works, but you're starting the engine, transmission, and all systems just to play a song. **Slice tests** are Spring Boot's focused testing annotations that load only the layer you're testing. @WebMvcTest loads controllers and MVC config, @DataJpaTest loads repositories and JPA, @JsonTest loads JSON serializers, @RestClientTest loads REST clients. Each slice excludes everything else, so tests start in 2-4 seconds instead of 10-15 seconds. You use @SpringBootTest when you genuinely need multiple layers working together—for example, testing that your controller correctly triggers a service that writes to the database and publishes a Kafka event. For isolated layer testing, slice tests are always faster and clearer.

sections.title: Full Context vs. Slice Tests Comparison
When to Choose Each Approach
sections.content: **Use @SpringBootTest when** you need to test cross-layer integration—for example, verifying that an HTTP request to your controller flows through security filters, calls a transactional service, writes to the database, and triggers an event listener. Also use it for testing scheduled jobs, startup listeners, or complex auto-configuration interactions. **Use slice tests when** you're testing a single layer in isolation. If you're testing controller request mapping and response serialization, use @WebMvcTest. If you're testing a custom JPA query or entity cascade behavior, use @DataJpaTest. If you're testing JSON serialization of a DTO, use @JsonTest. The key principle: **test at the narrowest scope that still validates what you need**. A faster test suite means developers run tests more often, catch bugs earlier, and stay in flow instead of waiting for slow builds.

sections.title: Key Points
content: **@SpringBootTest scope**: Loads entire application context including all beans, configs, and auto-configuration
**@WebMvcTest**: Loads only controllers, filters, exception handlers, and MVC config—mocks services
**@DataJpaTest**: Loads only repositories, entities, and embedded H2 database—no web or service layer
**@JsonTest**: Loads only JSON serialization/deserialization components for testing Jackson mappings
**Performance difference**: Slice tests start 3-5x faster than @SpringBootTest because they load fewer beans
**Test clarity**: Slice tests make it obvious what layer you're testing; @SpringBootTest tests can blur boundaries
**Integration tests**: Use @SpringBootTest for true end-to-end scenarios where multiple layers must interact

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: The key difference is scope and speed. At-SpringBootTest loads your entire application context—every bean, every auto-configuration, database connections, security setup, everything. It's like starting your whole car just to test the radio. It works, but it's slow, usually taking eight to fifteen seconds just to start. Slice tests, on the other hand, load only the layer you're testing. At-WebMvcTest loads just the web layer—controllers and MVC config—and mocks out services. At-DataJpaTest loads just the JPA layer with an embedded database, no controllers or services. At-JsonTest loads just the JSON serialization components. These slice tests start in two to four seconds because they're focused. You'd use at-SpringBootTest when you genuinely need an end-to-end integration test—for example, testing that an HTTP request flows through your security filters, triggers a service method with a transaction, writes to the database, and publishes an event. But for most tests, you're testing a single layer. If I'm testing a controller's request mapping and response format, I use at-WebMvcTest. If I'm testing a repository query, I use at-DataJpaTest. The big mistake freshers make is using at-SpringBootTest for everything because it's the first annotation they learned. That makes your test suite really slow, and slow tests mean developers run them less often, which defeats the purpose.

questions.question: What is the difference between @Mock and @MockBean in Spring Boot tests?
questions.title: @Mock vs @MockBean in Spring Boot
questions.direct_answer: @Mock is a pure Mockito annotation that creates a mock object with no Spring involvement—used in plain unit tests. @MockBean creates a mock and registers it as a Spring bean in the application context, replacing the real bean—used in Spring Boot tests like @WebMvcTest or @SpringBootTest.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand when to use each annotation and the performance cost of loading a Spring context just for mocking
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using @MockBean in a plain unit test that doesn't load Spring, which doesn't work and shows confusion about what each annotation does
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain that @MockBean forces Spring to rebuild the application context if the mock set changes, making tests slower, so use @Mock whenever you don't need Spring

sections.title: Mock vs. MockBean: Mockito and Spring Integration
sections.content: **@Mock is a pure Mockito annotation** that creates a mock object using Mockito's API, with no Spring framework involvement. You use it in **unit tests that don't load a Spring context**—tests annotated with @ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class) where you're testing a plain Java class. **@MockBean is a Spring Boot testing annotation** that creates a Mockito mock and registers it as a bean in the Spring application context, replacing any existing bean of that type. You use it in **Spring slice tests or integration tests** like @WebMvcTest or @SpringBootTest, where Spring is loading a context and you need to replace a real bean (like a service or repository) with a mock. Think of @Mock as **hiring a stunt double for a single scene:** no paperwork, no contracts, just a quick stand-in. @MockBean is like **adding the stunt double to the official cast list:** it requires updating the production roster (Spring context), which takes time. The key insight: if your test doesn't need Spring, use @Mock for speed. If Spring is already loading, use @MockBean to integrate the mock into that context.

sections.title: @Mock vs. @MockBean Feature Comparison
When to Use Each Annotation
sections.content: **Use @Mock when** you're writing a pure unit test that doesn't involve Spring at all. Your test class is annotated with @ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class), you're testing business logic in a service or utility class, and you just need to mock the dependencies that class uses. For example, testing OrderService unit logic with a mocked OrderRepository. **Use @MockBean when** your test loads a Spring context (annotated with @WebMvcTest, @DataJpaTest, @SpringBootTest, etc.) and you need to replace a real bean with a mock. For example, in a @WebMvcTest for a controller, you use @MockBean to mock the service the controller depends on, so Spring injects your mock instead of trying to load the real service (which doesn't exist in the web slice). **Important caveat:** if you change the set of @MockBean definitions in your test class, Spring must rebuild the entire application context, which can add 5-10 seconds to test startup. This is why you should prefer @Mock in unit tests—faster and no context overhead.

sections.title: Key Points
content: **@Mock**: Pure Mockito annotation, creates a mock with no Spring involvement, used in plain unit tests
**@MockBean**: Spring Boot annotation, creates a mock and registers it as a Spring bean, used in Spring tests
**Context dependency**: @Mock works without any context; @MockBean requires a Spring context to be loaded
**Performance**: @Mock is instant; @MockBean can trigger context rebuild if the mock set changes between test classes
**Injection**: @Mock mocks are injected via @InjectMocks; @MockBean mocks are injected by Spring's dependency injection
**Use case clarity**: If your test has no Spring annotation (like @WebMvcTest), use @Mock; if it does, use @MockBean
**Context caching**: Spring caches contexts by configuration; changing @MockBean beans invalidates the cache, slowing down tests

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: At-Mock and at-MockBean serve different purposes depending on whether you're loading a Spring context. At-Mock is a pure Mockito annotation—it creates a mock object with no Spring involvement at all. You use it in plain unit tests where you're just testing a Java class and you annotate the test with at-ExtendWith MockitoExtension. For example, if I'm unit testing an OrderService, I'd use at-Mock to create a mock OrderRepository, then at-InjectMocks to inject that mock into the service. No Spring context loads, so the test runs instantly. At-MockBean, on the other hand, is a Spring Boot testing annotation. It creates a Mockito mock and registers it as a Spring bean in the application context. You use it when your test loads a Spring context, like with at-WebMvcTest or at-SpringBootTest. For example, in a controller test with at-WebMvcTest, I'd use at-MockBean to mock the service the controller depends on. Spring then injects that mock into the controller instead of the real service. The important thing to know is that at-MockBean has a performance cost—if you change which beans are mocked, Spring has to rebuild the entire application context, which can add five to ten seconds. So the rule is: if your test doesn't load Spring, use at-Mock for speed. If it does load Spring, use at-MockBean to integrate the mock into that context.

questions.question: How do you test a Spring @Service that has a @Transactional method?
questions.title: Testing a @Transactional Spring Service
questions.direct_answer: For unit tests, mock the repository and test business logic without transactions—@Transactional has no effect without a Spring context. For integration tests, use @DataJpaTest or @SpringBootTest to load the transaction infrastructure, then verify transaction behavior like rollback on exceptions or cascade operations.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand that @Transactional is a Spring proxy behavior that only works when Spring's context is active, not in plain unit tests
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Trying to test transaction rollback in a unit test where no Spring context is loaded, expecting @Transactional to work without the transaction proxy
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain that unit tests focus on business logic and integration tests verify transaction behavior, and that @Transactional requires Spring's AOP proxy to function

sections.title: Testing Transactional Service Methods: Unit vs. Integration
sections.content: **The @Transactional annotation only works when Spring's application context is active** because it uses AOP proxies to intercept method calls and manage transaction boundaries. In a **unit test**, you mock the repository and test the service's business logic—input validation, calculations, exception handling—without any transaction behavior. The @Transactional annotation is present in the code but inactive because no Spring proxy exists. Think of it like **testing a car's steering without the engine running:** you can verify the steering wheel turns and the linkage moves, but you can't test whether it actually drives. In **integration tests** using @DataJpaTest or @SpringBootTest, Spring loads the transaction infrastructure, and @Transactional becomes active. Here you test transaction-specific behavior: rollback on exceptions, transaction propagation, cascade operations, and database constraints. The key insight is **separation of concerns:** unit tests verify logic, integration tests verify infrastructure behavior like transactions, database writes, and cross-layer coordination.

sections.title: Unit Test vs. Integration Test for Transactional Service
Key Points
content: **@Transactional requires Spring context**: The annotation only works when Spring's AOP proxy intercepts method calls
**Unit test scope**: Test business logic (validation, calculations) with mocked repositories—no transaction behavior
**Integration test scope**: Test transaction rollback, propagation, cascade operations with real database and Spring context
**Proxy mechanism**: Spring wraps your service in a proxy that starts/commits/rolls back transactions around @Transactional methods
**Rollback testing**: Use @DataJpaTest or @SpringBootTest to verify that exceptions trigger rollback and no data persists
**Test isolation**: Unit tests run in milliseconds without database; integration tests take seconds but verify real behavior
**When to verify**: Test transaction behavior when it's critical (e.g., payment processing), skip it for simple CRUD operations

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: Testing a transactional service method depends on what you're trying to verify. For unit tests, I focus on the business logic without worrying about transactions. I mock the repository using at-Mock and test things like input validation, exception handling, and calculations. In a unit test, the at-Transactional annotation is present in the service code but doesn't actually do anything because there's no Spring context loaded. Spring uses AOP proxies to intercept method calls and manage transactions, and those proxies don't exist in a plain unit test. It's like testing the steering wheel without starting the engine—you can verify the logic, but not the infrastructure behavior. For integration tests, I use at-DataJpaTest or at-SpringBootTest to load the Spring context and transaction infrastructure. Now at-Transactional is active. I can test that if the service method throws an exception, the transaction rolls back and no data is saved to the database. I'd insert some test data, trigger the exception, then assert that the repository count is still zero because the transaction was rolled back. The key is separating concerns: unit tests verify your business logic is correct, integration tests verify that the Spring transaction management and database interactions work as expected. A common mistake is trying to test rollback behavior in a unit test and wondering why it doesn't work—it's because the Spring proxy that manages transactions isn't there.

questions.question: How do you test a Spring @Service method that calls an external REST API?
questions.title: Testing Services with External REST Calls
questions.direct_answer: Mock the RestTemplate or WebClient dependency with @Mock, use when().thenReturn() to stub its HTTP methods (exchange, getForObject, etc.) with a test response, then assert that your service processes that response correctly. This keeps tests fast and doesn't depend on external APIs being available.

interviewer_intent.testing: Ability to isolate external HTTP dependencies in unit tests so tests are fast, deterministic, and don't require network access
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Letting the test make actual HTTP calls to external APIs, making tests slow, flaky, and dependent on external service availability
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention WireMock or MockWebServer for integration-level HTTP testing where you need more realistic request/response matching than Mockito provides

sections.title: Testing Services That Call External REST APIs
sections.content: **When your service depends on an external REST API, you mock the HTTP client (RestTemplate or WebClient) in unit tests.** You use **@Mock** to create a mock of the client, then stub its HTTP methods with **when().thenReturn()** to return a test response object. This keeps your test **fast (milliseconds), deterministic (no network flakiness), and isolated** (doesn't require the external API to be running). Think of it like **testing a weather app's display logic by feeding it fake weather data:** you don't need to call the real weather service to verify that your app correctly shows 'rainy' when it receives precipitation data. For **unit tests**, Mockito stubbing is sufficient—you're testing your service's logic given a specific API response. For **integration tests**, you'd use tools like **WireMock** or **MockWebServer** that start a real HTTP server on localhost and let you define request/response mappings. This tests the full HTTP interaction including serialization, headers, error handling, and retries.

sections.title: Unit Test for Service Calling External API
Key Points
content: **Mock the HTTP client**: Use @Mock on RestTemplate or WebClient—don't let tests call real external APIs
**Stub HTTP methods**: Use when().thenReturn() to stub postForObject, getForObject, exchange, etc. with test responses
**Response objects**: Create test instances of the response classes your service expects, with specific data for each scenario
**Argument matchers**: Use eq() for exact URL/body matching, any() for flexible matching, or ArgumentCaptor for assertions
**Error scenarios**: Test how your service handles null responses, HTTP errors, timeouts, and deserialization failures
**Integration alternative**: For more realistic HTTP testing, use WireMock or MockWebServer to stub an actual HTTP server
**No real calls**: Unit tests with mocked clients run in 10-50ms; real HTTP calls add 200-2000ms per test plus flakiness

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: I'd mock the RestTemplate or WebClient using Mockito so the test doesn't actually call the external API. First, I use at-Mock to create a mock of the HTTP client, and at-InjectMocks to inject it into the service. In the test method, I stub the client's HTTP method—like postForObject or getForObject—using when and thenReturn. I make it return a test response object that represents what the external API would return. For example, if my service calls a payment gateway, I'd create a test GatewayResponse object with an 'approved' status and a transaction ID, then stub restTemplate dot postForObject to return that. Then I call my service method and assert that it processes the response correctly—checking that it extracts the transaction ID, updates the order status, or whatever the business logic requires. I'd also test error cases, like when the API returns null or throws an exception, by using thenReturn null or thenThrow. This approach keeps tests really fast because there's no network call—the test runs in milliseconds. It's also deterministic; you don't have flaky failures because the external API is down or slow. For more advanced integration tests, I'd mention WireMock or MockWebServer, which let you start a real HTTP server in the test and define request-response mappings. That's useful when you need to test things like retry logic or complex response scenarios, but for unit tests, pure Mockito stubbing is the right tool.

questions.question: How do you test exception handling in a Spring @Service — for example, when a repository throws a DataAccessException?
questions.title: Testing Exception Handling in Spring Services
questions.direct_answer: Stub the mock to throw the exception using when().thenThrow(), then use assertThrows() from JUnit 5 to verify that your service throws the expected exception or handles it correctly. Test both propagation (service re-throws) and translation (service wraps the exception in a domain-specific exception).

interviewer_intent.testing: Ability to write negative-path tests that cover error handling code, ensuring your service behaves correctly when dependencies fail
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Only testing the happy path and leaving exception handling branches untested, resulting in low code coverage and unverified error logic
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Show both the case where the service propagates the exception unchanged and the case where it translates/wraps it into a custom domain exception with context

sections.title: Testing Exception Handling in Spring Services
sections.content: **Exception handling tests verify that your service correctly responds when dependencies fail.** You use **when().thenThrow()** to make your mock throw a specific exception, then use **assertThrows()** from JUnit 5 to verify that your service throws the expected exception type. There are two common patterns: **propagation** (the service lets the exception bubble up unchanged) and **translation** (the service catches the lower-level exception and throws a domain-specific exception with added context). Think of exception handling like **smoke detectors in a building:** you're testing that the alarm goes off correctly, that it shuts down the right systems, and that it provides useful information (not just 'something went wrong'). Testing exceptions is critical because **error paths are often less tested in production** but frequently executed in real failure scenarios—database timeouts, network failures, constraint violations. A well-tested exception flow logs the right details, returns the right HTTP status, and preserves error messages for debugging.

sections.title: Testing Exception Handling with Propagation and Translation
Key Points
content: **when().thenThrow()**: Stubs the mock to throw a specific exception when the method is called with matching arguments
**assertThrows()**: JUnit 5 assertion that verifies the code block throws the expected exception type and returns the exception instance
**Exception propagation**: Service lets the exception bubble up unchanged—useful for infrastructure exceptions like DataAccessException
**Exception translation**: Service catches low-level exception and throws a domain-specific exception with added context (e.g., order ID)
**Message assertions**: Verify the exception message contains useful debugging information like entity IDs or operation details
**Verify no side effects**: Use verify(mock, never()).method() to assert that the error case prevented unwanted operations
**Coverage importance**: Exception paths are critical for production reliability but often under-tested in happy-path-focused test suites

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: I'd use Mockito's when and thenThrow to make the mock throw the exception, then use assertThrows from JUnit 5 to verify my service handles it correctly. For example, if I'm testing how OrderService handles a database failure, I'd stub the repository mock to throw a DataAccessException using when orderRepository dot findById then thenThrow. Then I call the service method inside an assertThrows block and verify that it throws the expected exception type. There are usually two patterns. First is propagation, where the service just lets the exception bubble up unchanged. For example, if the repository throws DataAccessException, the service might let that propagate to the controller, where a global exception handler converts it to a 500 error. The second pattern is translation, where the service catches the low-level exception and throws a more meaningful domain exception. For instance, if the repository returns an empty Optional, the service throws OrderNotFoundException with a message like 'Order not found: ID 999.' This gives better context for debugging. I'd also test that when an exception occurs, no side effects happen—for example, using verify with never to assert that the repository's save method was never called. Testing exception handling is really important because error paths are often less tested but frequently hit in production when things go wrong—database timeouts, network failures, constraint violations. A good test verifies not just that the exception is thrown, but that the error message is useful and the system didn't leave data in an inconsistent state.
